newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD - Capex the key for Australian markets.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Capex the key for Australian markets.

text.p: Today's third quarter capital expenditure report, especially data on business investment intentions, holds the key to Australian markets this week as it could determine if another interest rate cut on the cards.
The latest report on enterprise bargaining agreements may also be released by the Department of Industrial Relations.
Both reports were given high priority in last month's Reserve Bank quarterly Bulletin and analysts believe that any signs of weakness could fuel hopes of cut in rates.
Forecasts centre on a fall of 3.0 percent but views are wildly divergent, ranging from a rise of 2.5 percent to a fall of 15 percent in a Reuters poll of 32 economists.
Balance of payments data for October are also due on Friday but are not expected to have much impact unless they are way out of range of the expected deficit of $A1.6 billion.
BONDS (Fri 10 yr cash yield 7.05 pct, 3-yr 6.38 pct)
The week is brewing as a key one for the local debt market and could determine whether its 2-1/2 month rally is nearing conclusion or whether a further erosion in yields is possible.

Analysts said the Australian dollar's rush to six-year highs last week was effectively a tightening in policy just when the authorities were keen to set the easier monetary conditions to ensure a pick-up in the economy.
Long-dated bond yields brushed 33-month lows on Friday as short-dated bonds and bill futures built in the possibility of an easing on the dollar's strength.
U.S. Treasuries offer little in the way of a lead.
U.S. bonds ended flat to lower across the yield curve in extremely dull trading. The yield on the 30-year benchmark T-bond closed slightly higher at 6.44 percent.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri US$0.8085/90, New York $0.8142/47)
A weak Capex report could also give the high flying dollar some pause, although traders thought a bullish outlook was pretty well assured after the break of six-year highs last week.

"While the A$ is likely to consolidate after rising by 1.9 U.S. cents, there exists clear underlying support for the currency at around 80 U.S. cents," Macquarie Bank economists said in a weekly market commentary.

Chart followers were extremely upbeat on the currency and were tipping a sustained rally through US$0.8150 to an eventual target of US$0.8450. Only a breach of US$0.7950 would trouble that view, they said.
Further yen/A$ samurai issues were also expected in the run-up to year-end as Japanese workers received traditional bonuses and funneled some of those funds into higher yielding assets offshore.

Signs of fragility in the Japanese banking system last week suggested the chances of a hike in interest rates was slim but the risk could return if the Bank of Japan's Tankan survey of business sentiment on Wednesday proves stronger than expected.
The Australian current account data should not trouble the currency unless the deficit blow out to A$2.0 billion or more.
AUSTRALIAN SHARES (Fri All Ordinaries 2383.4, down 9.1)
Stocks are getting mixed signals.
The Dow jumped another 53.29 points to 6471.76 on Friday but copper and gold prices fell in overseas trading.

Equity market players see the week ahead as mixed with little in the way of corporate news to encourage local investors to step into the market, although there still seemed to be substantial interest from offshore funds looking for a home.
"What has been driving our market at the moment is there has been a reasonable flow of (offshore) funds," said Derek Bond, director at Burrell and Co. He said this was set to continue.
"Obviously, these mutual funds in the U.S. are still fairly flush and I think you are not going to see those funds continue to go into the U.S. market," he said.
"Probably, you are going to see fund managers take the view over there that they have to look around elsewhere."
With the annual meetings season all but over and the major banks having posted their annual results, some brokers believe things may now start to wind down in the run-up to Christmas.
The obvious exceptions to this will be how investors treat Wall Street's seemingly unstoppable record run and the ability of base metals prices to stand their ground.
"I'm pretty cautious to be honest," Bond said.
Annual meetings of note this week include nickel venturer Anaconda Nickel on Monday and retailers Harvey Norman and Just Jeans on Tuesday.
